split_question: Should the Government help households with the January rise in the energy price cap?
angles: Help only the poorest, by need
No new help: let the market price stand
facts_for_writers: The current cap is £1,723 a year for a typical household and the predicted January cap is about £2,184, but Ofgem has not yet announced it (s1).
The Joseph Rowntree Foundation says the £400 rebate in the last crisis cost £11.9 billion, and proposes a £6.3 billion winter package to cut average bills by about £230 (s3).

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation says taking the remaining Renewables Obligation, Feed-in Tariff and Warm Home Discount costs off electricity bills is worth about £60 a year to the average household (s3).

Energy UK, a trade body, says the Government spent £36 billion on universal household support in 2022/23 and calls that an inefficient use of public funds; it wants extra targeted help on top of the Warm Home Discount (s4).
Energy UK projects household energy debt reaching £7 billion by the end of 2026 (s4).
